claims.claim: Databricks Asset Bundles were renamed Declarative Automation Bundles on 16 March 2026; the change is non-breaking.
databricks.yml structure: bundle, variables, resources.jobs with parameters and tasks, targets with mode; variable resolution order.
Development mode prefixes resources with [dev ${workspace.current_user.short_name}] and pauses schedules and triggers.
Notebook tasks read job parameters with dbutils.widgets.get.

concept_html:
A job built by clicking in the UI exists only in one workspace, with no history and no review. Declarative Automation Bundles describe jobs, their tasks, parameters and notifications as YAML files in your repository. Databricks renamed them from Databricks Asset Bundles on 16 March 2026. The databricks bundle commands and databricks.yml did not change.

A bundle has one databricks.yml at its root:

bundle:
  name: research_pipelines

variables:
  catalog:
    description: Catalog the pipelines write to.

resources:
  jobs:
    nat_silver_pipeline:
      name: nat_silver_pipeline
      parameters:
        - name: catalog
          default: ${var.catalog}
      tasks:
        - task_key: silver
          notebook_task:
            notebook_path: ./notebooks/silver_nat_transform.py

targets:
  dev:
    mode: development
    default: true
    variables:
      catalog: research_dev
  prod:
    mode: production
    variables:
      catalog: research_prod
  • Targets are environments. One code base deploys to each with different values.
  • Variables hold what differs per target. They resolve from --var, then BUNDLE_VAR_ environment variables, then target mappings, then defaults.
  • Job parameters reach notebook tasks, which read them with dbutils.widgets.get("catalog"). Dynamic references such as {{job.run_id}} fill in values at run time.
  • mode: development prefixes job names with [dev <your name>] and pauses schedules, so your test deployment never runs on the production timetable.

The commands:

databricks bundle validate -t dev
databricks bundle deploy -t dev
databricks bundle run -t dev nat_silver_pipeline

Deploy to prod only from CI, as a service principal (lesson A10-L3).

exercises.prompt_html: The notebook for this job must read its catalog and wave_id job parameters. Write read_job_parameters(widgets): widgets behaves like dbutils.widgets (it has .get(name)). Return a dict with both values. Raise ValueError when catalog is not research_dev or research_prod, or when wave_id is empty.
exercises.solution:
ALLOWED_CATALOGS = {"research_dev", "research_prod"}


def read_job_parameters(widgets: object) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Read and validate the job parameters passed to this notebook.

    Args:
        widgets: dbutils.widgets, or any object with get(name).

    Returns:
        catalog and wave_id.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the catalog is not allowed or wave_id is empty.
    """
    get = getattr(widgets, "get")
    catalog = str(get("catalog"))
    wave_id = str(get("wave_id")).strip()
    if catalog not in ALLOWED_CATALOGS:
        raise ValueError(f"catalog {catalog!r} is not one of {sorted(ALLOWED_CATALOGS)}")
    if not wave_id:
        raise ValueError("wave_id is empty")
    return {"catalog": catalog, "wave_id": wave_id}

title: Declarative Automation Bundles and parameterised jobs
why_html:
A team manages its jobs in the UI. Someone changes the production silver job's notebook path to test a branch, meaning to change it back. They forget. For a week, production runs a half-finished branch. Nobody can say what changed or when, because the UI keeps no diff and nothing was reviewed.

With the job in a bundle, the path is a line in databricks.yml. Changing it needs a pull request, CI validates it, and Git shows exactly what changed.
